idiom_name: operator fun iterator(): Iterator<T> + hasNext()/next(), driven by for loops
implementation_notes: Kotlin exposes the protocol through operator conventions: a type defines operator fun iterator(): Iterator<T> (the stdlib Iterator declares abstract hasNext()/next(); remove() has a default only to satisfy the JDK's Iterator), and a for loop expands to the hasNext/next pair, so the classic roles disappear behind language syntax. Collections already implement it; implement Iterator/Iterable yourself for custom containers, or use the Iterable { } / iterator { } builders to wrap a suspended sequence of values. For operations that need no explicit cursor, stdlib extensions (map/filter/fold over Iterable) are the shorter path.
pitfalls: Iterator state is mutable and one-shot: an exhausted iterator silently keeps returning false from hasNext(), and building an iterator over an immutable source makes remove() throw UnsupportedOperationException.
The Java collections' fail-fast ConcurrentModificationException still leaks through Kotlin's read-only interfaces, so modifying a list inside a for loop over it is a runtime trap.
A sequence/iterator should not be shared across coroutines or threads; hasNext/next is a non-atomic pair, so interleaved access loses or duplicates elements.

variants.name: Sequence lazy pipelines
variants.idiom_name: Sequence + sequence { yield() } builder + asSequence() chains
variants.implementation_notes: Sequences are the lazy counterpart of Iterable: intermediate operations (map/filter/take) return another Sequence and are applied per element only when a terminal operation (toList/sum/first) iterates, which avoids materializing intermediate collections and permits infinite sources. The sequence { } builder with yield/yieldAll (Kotlin 1.3, built on suspend) and asSequence() turn existing code into a lazy traversal; constrainOnce() marks genuinely single-shot sequences, and custom sequences implement operator fun iterator(). Use sequences for long or chained pipelines over large data and plain Iterable for small collections, where the per-element wrapper overhead dominates.
pitfalls: Sequences are cold: the pipeline re-runs on every terminal operation and sees mutations made in between, and a constrained-once sequence throws when iterator() is called a second time.
Each lazy step adds a wrapper object and per-element dispatch, which measurably loses to eager Iterable chains for small collections and simple pipelines.
take(4) over an infinite generateSequence/sequence{} builder terminates only because of the terminal operation; without one, an infinite sequence hangs the consumer.
